title: Noah and the Pigeon Predicament
markdown:
Sunbeams, big and bold as paint strokes, stretched across Noah’s bedroom floor. He bounced out of bed already holding the notepad he used for scientific quests, pencil poised. Today: Oakwood Station, Auntie Jo, and Maple coming too. Maple’s long ears twitched. Her nose worked the morning as if it were a list.

They had a plan. The Sunbeam Express, polished as a penny, departed at ten o’clock. Auntie Jo needed a tiny ticking gadget that could measure the speed of clouds. Noah had promised, firm nod, that he would bring it.

Breakfast was swift: orange juice, buttery toast. Outside the air was crisp, dewdrops glittering on the garden path. He grabbed the bicycle. Maple perched in her woven basket, ears like tiny flags.

“Left at the big oak, then straight past the bakery,” Noah chanted.

Then the path filled. A colossal flock of pigeons decided on a dance party in the exact middle — grey feathers, flapping, an estimated one billion if you asked Noah before he had counted. They turned, they bowed, they took the whole width of the lane as if they had booked it. He braked hard. The bike skidded on the damp. Maple gave a tiny squeak and flattened her ears until the nearest pigeon finished a spin.

His watch: 9:40. The pigeons had eaten minutes. The Express. The gadget. Auntie Jo’s window in his head, already looking for him. “A proper pickle.” He waited for a gap, then pushed the pedals. Pant, pant, pant. A stray feather stuck to the handlebar. The bakery smell arrived and left, warm and useless as a clock with no hands. The oak fell behind. Maple’s basket bounced; he put a steadying hand on her back without slowing.

They skidded to a stop outside Oakwood Station. The clock tower’s hands: 9:52. “Just in time.” He grabbed Maple and the package. Through the doors: bustle, booming announcements, trains hissing like sleepy dragons.

The departure board was a giant puzzle of towns and times. Noah’s eyes went watch, board, watch. Sunbeam Express, Platform 3, 10:00 — still there, still true. A porter checked his own watch with calm precision and did not run, which was information of a sort. A sign said *Next train to Meadowbrook: 10:15* — a different train, a different gleam, useful only as a warning not to board the wrong hiss. Noah watched the tower: each large number five minutes, the second hand tick-tick-tick, a march that did not care about pigeons.

“Our train leaves at 10:00. We got here at 9:52. Eight minutes.” He counted them on his fingers once, then on the clock face, hopping from 52 to 00 the long way around the twelve. A hurried lady rushed past and missed a departing train by a whisker, flustered as a closed door. Noah felt the eight minutes sit in his chest, countable. “Elapsed time. How much has passed. How much is left.” Maple’s ear flicked, which he took for agreement.

“Come on, Maple.” They dashed for Platform 3. The Sunbeam Express waited, golden, and Auntie Jo was already waving from a window, smile wide.

They scrambled aboard as the whistle blew a cheerful toot-toot. A cozy empty spot by the window, still warm from someone who had chosen a different platform. The ticking package tucked beside them, gadget safe, promise kept. Noah did not declare that the adventure had just begun. He wrote in the notepad, still a little out of breath:

Left house — pigeons — 9:40.
Station — 9:52. Twelve minutes eaten.
Train — 10:00. Eight minutes remaining.

Maple twitched her nose. Noah stroked her fur and watched the platform slide away. Understanding a timetable was not the same as hoping. The clouds, when Auntie Jo measured them, would have to keep their own time. The gadget ticked in agreement, or perhaps only ticked.
